inputs.original_text: Cyprus is moving toward a surveillance law that would weaken judicial oversight—the kind of safeguard that matters most when state power is used against people with the least ability to challenge it. Lawyers are warning ahead of Thursday’s House vote, but this is not just a technical legal change: without independent scrutiny, surveillance can deepen existing inequalities and leave vulnerable communities especially exposed. The state should not be trusted to police itself. The bill should not be approved without real transparency and strong safeguards.
inputs.modified_text: Cyprus is heading toward a surveillance law that would reduce judicial oversight, despite lawyers’ warnings before Thursday’s House vote. That is not a minor procedural change: when the state can monitor people without strong independent checks, those with the least power to defend themselves are most at risk. Surveillance can reinforce existing inequality and put vulnerable communities under greater pressure. The state cannot be its own watchdog; the bill should not pass without genuine transparency and enforceable safeguards.
